lede: Heat blue copper(II) sulfate and it turns white; add water and the blue comes back. Some reactions run both ways, the conditions decide the direction, and in a sealed container the two directions settle into a balance.
can: Explain what reversible means and write the equation with its sign.
Describe the copper(II) sulfate test in both directions.
Define dynamic equilibrium, rates first and amounts second.

md: Most reactions you have met run one way and stop. A few run both ways: the products can turn back into the reactants, and the conditions decide which way the reaction goes. Blue crystals that turn white when heated, and blue again when water is added, are the example to keep in mind.

md: A **reversible reaction** is one in which the **products can change back into the reactants**. Heat blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate and it loses its water; add the water back and the blue crystals re-form. Burning magnesium is not reversible: no change of conditions turns magnesium oxide back into magnesium and oxygen. A reversible reaction is written with the sign $\ce{<=>}$, never a single arrow.

title: Why the sign earns its own mark
md: A one-way arrow says the reaction finishes and the reactants are gone. The reversible sign says something different: both reactions are happening, so reactants and products are present together. The symbol is the claim, which is why schemes give it its own mark.

stem: Nitrogen dioxide, $\ce{NO2}$, forms dinitrogen tetroxide, $\ce{N2O4}$, in a reversible reaction. (a) Give a balanced symbol equation, with the reversible sign. [4] (b) What is meant by a reversible reaction? [1]

steps.decision: Formulae first. The reactant goes on the left; its formula is given, so copy it exactly.
The product goes on the right, as a separate mark from the left-hand side.

steps.working: Balance: $\ce{2NO2}$, because one $\ce{N2O4}$ holds 2 N atoms and 4 O atoms.
steps.decision: Count each element on both sides; a big number in front multiplies the whole formula.
The reversible sign is a mark of its own: a single arrow claims the reaction goes one way only.

steps.working: (b) The product, dinitrogen tetroxide, can change back into the reactant, nitrogen dioxide.
steps.decision: Name products and reactants. 'It can be reversed' or 'it returns to its original state' earns nothing.

prompt: Which symbol is used in the equation for a reversible reaction?
explain: The reversible sign, two half-arrows pointing opposite ways, claims both directions at once, as step 4 of See it wrote it. A single arrow claims the reaction runs one way and finishes, and an equals sign belongs in maths, not in a chemical equation.

optionNotes.why: The arrow of an ordinary equation claims the reaction runs one way and finishes; a reversible reaction does not.
An equals sign belongs in a maths equation; a chemical equation needs an arrow or the reversible sign.

twin.prompt: In the equation for a reversible reaction, what does the ⇌ sign tell you?
options: both the forward and the reverse reaction can happen
the reaction has stopped
the reaction gives out heat
twin.answer: both the forward and the reverse reaction can happen
twin.explain: The two half-arrows point both ways: the reactants can form the products and the products can re-form the reactants, as step 4 of See it showed.

optionNotes.option: the reaction has stopped
optionNotes.why: Nothing in the sign says a reaction has stopped; it says both directions are possible.

optionNotes.option: the reaction gives out heat
optionNotes.why: The sign says nothing about heat; an energy change is shown by a temperature change or a profile.

prompt: A student writes that a reversible reaction is 'a reaction that can be reversed'. Why does this not earn the mark?
options: it never says the products can change back into the reactants
it should say the reaction returns to its original state
it should give an example that uses a catalyst
answer: it never says the products can change back into the reactants
explain: The mark is for the products changing back into the reactants, named as step 5 of See it wrote it. 'Can be reversed' only repeats the word being defined, and 'original state' names neither the products nor the reactants.

optionNotes.option: it should say the reaction returns to its original state
optionNotes.why: 'Original state' names neither the products nor the reactants, and the 2025 report says it lost the mark.

optionNotes.option: it should give an example that uses a catalyst
optionNotes.why: A catalyst has nothing to do with whether a reaction is reversible; the definition is about products and reactants.

twin.prompt: A student writes that a reversible reaction 'goes back to its original state'. Why does this lose the mark?
options: it names neither the products nor the reactants
it should say the reaction can be reversed
it forgets to mention the reversible sign
twin.answer: it names neither the products nor the reactants
twin.explain: The scheme wants the products changing back into the reactants, both named, as step 5 of See it wrote it; 'original state' names neither.

optionNotes.option: it should say the reaction can be reversed
optionNotes.why: 'Can be reversed' only repeats the word; it earns nothing either.

optionNotes.option: it forgets to mention the reversible sign
optionNotes.why: The sign belongs in an equation; a definition in words needs the products and reactants named.

text: 2. The copper(II) sulfate test, both ways

md: **Heat** blue **hydrated copper(II) sulfate** and the water bonded in its crystals is driven off as steam, leaving **white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate**. **Add water** to the white powder and it turns **blue** again, and the tube **gets hot**. In words: hydrated copper(II) sulfate $\ce{<=>}$ anhydrous copper(II) sulfate + water.

title: Colours the scheme accepts
md: Give both colours whenever you describe a change: **white to blue** on adding water, **blue to white** on heating. One colour on its own earns nothing, and 'clear' or 'colourless' is not white.

stem: Adding water to white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate makes the tube hot. (a) Is the reaction with water exothermic or endothermic? [1] (b) What must happen to heat when the blue crystals are heated to turn them white again? [1]

steps.working: (a) Exothermic: heat is given out, so the tube gets hot.
steps.decision: The warm tube is the evidence; heat given out is what exothermic means.

steps.working: (b) Heat must be taken in: the reverse reaction is endothermic.
steps.decision: A reversible reaction that gives out heat one way takes the same amount in the other way.

steps.working: So the blue crystals must be heated to turn white: the flame supplies the heat that direction takes in.
steps.decision: The heating is not only to speed things up; the reverse direction needs that energy.

title: GCSE Chemistry Revision "Reversible Reactions"
why: The blue-to-white change run both ways, beside our own steps.

prompt: Ammonium chloride splits into ammonia and hydrogen chloride when heated, and the two gases join to form ammonium chloride again as they cool. The splitting takes heat in. What does the joining do?
options: it gives out heat
it takes heat in as well
it has no energy change
explain: A reversible reaction that takes heat in one way gives the same heat out the other way. Step 2 of See it showed it for copper(II) sulfate: adding water gave heat out, so heating the crystals took it in.

optionNotes.option: it takes heat in as well
optionNotes.why: Both directions cannot take heat in: whatever one direction takes in, the other gives back out.

optionNotes.option: it has no energy change
optionNotes.why: The splitting takes heat in, so the reverse cannot be zero: it gives the same amount out.

twin.prompt: Nitrogen dioxide forms dinitrogen tetroxide and gives out heat. What happens to heat when dinitrogen tetroxide turns back into nitrogen dioxide?
options: heat is taken in
heat is given out as well
no heat is involved
twin.explain: Heat out one way means the same heat in the other way, as step 2 of See it showed for copper(II) sulfate.

optionNotes.option: heat is given out as well
optionNotes.why: If both directions gave heat out, energy would appear from nowhere; one gives out, the other takes in.

optionNotes.option: no heat is involved
optionNotes.why: The forward reaction gives out heat, so the reverse cannot be zero: it takes that heat back in.

md: Start a reversible reaction in a **sealed** vessel. The forward reaction begins fast and slows as its reactants are used up; the reverse reaction begins at zero and speeds up as the products build. When the two **rates become equal**, the reaction is at **dynamic equilibrium**: each substance is made as fast as it is used up, so the **amounts of reactants and products stay constant**.

title: Why it is called dynamic
md: Nothing has stopped: both reactions are still running, at the same rate as each other. It only looks still from outside, because nothing changes overall. Equal rates, not equal amounts: the amounts themselves are usually quite different from each other.

stem: The graph shows the rates of the forward and reverse reactions for a reaction in a sealed flask. (a) At what time is equilibrium reached? [1] (b) What is true of the two rates from then on? [1] (c) Explain why the amounts of reactants and products then stay constant. [1]

steps.working: (a) At 30 s, where the two curves meet.
steps.decision: Read along the time axis to the point where the solid and the dashed lines join.

steps.working: (b) The rates are equal: both are 5 from 30 s on.
steps.decision: Equal rates is the first half of the definition, and neither rate falls to zero.

steps.working: (c) Each substance is made as fast as it is used up, so its amount stays constant.
steps.decision: The constant amounts follow from the equal rates: say the rates first, then what that does to the amounts.

prompt: On a rate–time graph for a reaction in a sealed flask, the forward and reverse rates meet at 25 s and then run together. What happens to the amounts of reactants and products after 25 s?
options: they stay constant
they become equal to each other
they both fall to zero
explain: From the moment the rates are equal, each substance is made as fast as it is used up, so its amount stays the same: step 3 of See it. The amounts are not equal to each other, and nothing falls to zero because both reactions keep running.

optionNotes.option: they become equal to each other
optionNotes.why: Equal rates, not equal amounts: the amounts stop changing at whatever values they have reached.

optionNotes.option: they both fall to zero
optionNotes.why: Both reactions keep running at equilibrium, so neither the reactants nor the products run out.

twin.prompt: On the same kind of graph, the two rates meet at 80 s. Which statement is true at 40 s?
options: the forward rate is still greater than the reverse rate
the amounts of reactants and products are constant
the two rates are equal
twin.answer: the forward rate is still greater than the reverse rate
twin.explain: Before the curves meet, the forward rate is still falling towards the reverse rate, which is still rising, as the graph in See it showed before its meeting point.

optionNotes.option: the amounts of reactants and products are constant
optionNotes.why: The amounts only stop changing once the rates are equal, which is later, at the meeting point.

optionNotes.option: the two rates are equal
optionNotes.why: They are only equal from the meeting point on; before it the forward rate is the larger.

md: Dynamic equilibrium needs a **closed system**: nothing can get in or out. Heat limestone in an open tube and the carbon dioxide escapes into the room, so it can never react with the calcium oxide to re-form calcium carbonate. The reverse reaction never keeps pace and the rates never become equal. In a sealed tube the carbon dioxide stays, so both reactions can run.

stem: Calcium carbonate is heated in a sealed tube and in an open tube: $\ce{CaCO3 <=> CaO + CO2}$. Explain why only the sealed tube can reach a dynamic equilibrium. [2]

steps.working: In the open tube the carbon dioxide escapes, so it cannot react with the calcium oxide.
steps.decision: Name what escapes: a gas leaving is what stops the reverse reaction.

steps.working: So the reverse reaction cannot keep pace and the rates never become equal; in the sealed tube nothing escapes, so they can.
steps.decision: Finish with the rates: equilibrium is defined by them, so the explanation has to reach them.

prompt: A reversible reaction that makes a gas is carried out in an open beaker. Why can it never reach a dynamic equilibrium?
options: the gas escapes, so the reverse reaction cannot keep pace
the temperature keeps changing
the forward reaction stops at once
answer: the gas escapes, so the reverse reaction cannot keep pace
explain: A product that escapes cannot react back, so the reverse rate never catches up with the forward rate, as step 1 of See it said of the carbon dioxide from limestone. Sealing the vessel keeps every substance in.

optionNotes.option: the temperature keeps changing
optionNotes.why: A closed system is about substances getting in or out, not about heat.

optionNotes.option: the forward reaction stops at once
optionNotes.why: The forward reaction keeps going; it is the reverse reaction that cannot keep pace once a product escapes.

twin.prompt: The same kind of reaction is carried out in a stoppered flask instead. Why can it now reach a dynamic equilibrium?
options: the gas cannot escape, so the reverse reaction can keep pace
the stopper keeps the heat in
the stopper stops the forward reaction
twin.answer: the gas cannot escape, so the reverse reaction can keep pace
twin.explain: With nothing escaping, the product stays and reacts back until the two rates are equal, as step 2 of See it said of the sealed tube.

optionNotes.option: the stopper keeps the heat in
optionNotes.why: Keeping heat in is not the reason: a closed system stops substances escaping.

optionNotes.option: the stopper stops the forward reaction
optionNotes.why: Both reactions keep running in a stoppered flask; that is what makes the equilibrium dynamic.

caption: Push the plunger and the pressure rises; the colour of the gas changes because the direction does.

md: Changing the **temperature**, the **pressure** or the **concentration** of a reactant or product changes the **direction** of a reversible reaction, and so changes the amounts of reactants and products present. Learn all three as a set: most candidates name temperature and stop (2025 report).

title: Where this specification stops
md: Other boards ask which way the reaction shifts, using Le Chatelier's principle. CCEA's Double Award stops at 'the direction changes': you are never asked to predict which way.

stem: Brown nitrogen dioxide and colourless dinitrogen tetroxide are at equilibrium in a sealed syringe: $\ce{2NO2 <=> N2O4}$. The plunger is pushed in and the colour of the gas changes. (a) Name the condition that was changed. [1] (b) What does the colour change show? [1]

steps.decision: Pushing the plunger squeezes the same gas into a smaller space, which raises the pressure.

steps.working: (b) The amounts of nitrogen dioxide and dinitrogen tetroxide have changed: the direction of the reaction changed.
steps.decision: A colour change means a change in amounts. CCEA asks only that the direction changes, not which way.

prompt: A reversible reaction is at dynamic equilibrium in a sealed flask. More of one reactant is added. What happens?
options: the direction changes, so the amounts of reactants and products change
nothing changes, because it is at equilibrium
both reactions stop
answer: the direction changes, so the amounts of reactants and products change
explain: Concentration is one of the three conditions, with temperature and pressure: altering it changes the direction, and so the amounts, as the colour in step 2 of See it showed. An equilibrium is not frozen; it responds to a change.

optionNotes.option: nothing changes, because it is at equilibrium
optionNotes.why: Equilibrium only means the rates are equal now; change a condition and the direction changes.

optionNotes.option: both reactions stop
optionNotes.why: Neither reaction stops; the balance between them shifts until the rates are equal again.

twin.prompt: A reversible reaction at dynamic equilibrium in a sealed flask is cooled. Which statement is right?
options: the amounts change, because the direction of the reaction changes
cooling cannot change a reaction at equilibrium
only the forward reaction slows, so the amounts stay the same
twin.answer: the amounts change, because the direction of the reaction changes
twin.explain: Temperature is one of the three conditions that change the direction, and a changed direction changes the amounts, as step 2 of See it showed for pressure.

optionNotes.option: cooling cannot change a reaction at equilibrium
optionNotes.why: Temperature is one of the three conditions that change the direction of a reversible reaction.

optionNotes.option: only the forward reaction slows, so the amounts stay the same
optionNotes.why: If the rates stop being equal the amounts must change; they stay constant only while the rates match.

md:
**Tick two statements** (2021, 2022). A list of six or eight; two are true: the rates are equal, and the amounts stay constant. The traps are amounts equal, both reactions stopped, and half reactants, half products.
**Complete the sentence** (2025). Two gaps, one for the rates and one for the amounts: rates first, amounts second.

**Why constant?** (2024). 'Explain why the amounts remain constant' wants the rates: the forward and reverse rates are equal. Saying the concentration does not change only repeats the question.
**The sign and the states** (2024, 2026). An equilibrium equation needs $\ce{<=>}$, and state symbols when they are asked for.
**Temperature** (2025). Changing it changes the direction, and so the amounts.

stem: The reaction $\ce{2NO2 <=> N2O4}$ has reached dynamic equilibrium in a sealed syringe. Explain why the amount of dinitrogen tetroxide stays constant. [1]

steps.working: The forward reaction makes dinitrogen tetroxide and the reverse reaction uses it up, both all the time.
steps.decision: Start from what is still happening: both reactions run.

steps.working: The forward and reverse reactions run at the same rate, so it is made as fast as it is used up.
steps.decision: The mark is for the equal rates. 'Its concentration does not change' only repeats the question (2024 report).

prompt: A reaction is at dynamic equilibrium in a sealed flask. The forward reaction makes 0.6 g of product every second. How many grams of product does the reverse reaction use up every second?
explain: Equal rates means the product is used up exactly as fast as it is made: 0.6 g every second. That is why its amount stays constant, step 2 of See it.

twin.prompt: At dynamic equilibrium in a sealed flask, the forward reaction uses up 1.5 g of reactant every second. How many grams of reactant does the reverse reaction re-form every second?
twin.explain: The rates are equal, so the reactant is re-formed as fast as it is used up: 1.5 g every second, as in step 2 of See it.

md:
Say what reversible means: the products can change back into the reactants.
Write the equation with ⇌, and give the copper(II) sulfate test both ways.
Define dynamic equilibrium: in a closed system, rates equal, amounts constant.
Explain why the system must be closed: nothing escapes, so both reactions run.
Name the three conditions that change the direction: temperature, pressure, concentration.

Equilibrium is in every C2 paper: a few marks at Foundation (the sign, a condition, what reversible means) and 4 to 8 marks at Higher, as Q2, Q4, Q7 or Q8 since 2019. The first mark is often the reversible sign; the definition is rates first, amounts second. Stuck? Write what is equal, then what is constant.
